extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors / patent attorneys, docketing patent drafters, and inventors involved in claim drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for when and how to draft Markush (alternative/group-selection) patent claims, including accepted claim wordings, limits on their use, and best practices to avoid rejections. Focused on claim-drafting decisions during patent prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve claim count / financial consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a Markush claim to conserve the number of separate claims required because standard non-provisional filing fees include only twenty total claims (three of which may be independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Markush claim allows grouping multiple alternatives into one claim (e.g., listing multiple species in one clause) instead of filing multiple dependent claims, which can save fees and avoid exceeding the allotted claim count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use when a subgroup lacks a proper nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim is appropriate when the sub-group of alternatives has no proper nomenclature to identify it, so the claim must create a generic name for that subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: listing a subset of alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) as 'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of...' creates a usable subgroup name when no established term exists for that subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across 35 U.S.C. §101 statutory classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claiming may be used with any of the recognized statutory classes — processes, machines, articles of manufacture, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, for many mechanical and method inventions, a 'means for' or 'step for' claim (where a generic functional term exists) may be an alternative to Markush claiming; such 'means/step for' claims are governed by 35 U.S.C. §112(f). Choose Markush where no suitable generic term exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted Markush claim forms (closed-group wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: One accepted form: use 'selected from the group consisting of ...' together with the conjunctive 'and' to denote a closed group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
The 'consisting of' + 'and' form indicates a closed list and helps avoid indefiniteness rejections. Example layout shown in the article:
'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of lithium, sodium, and potassium'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted Markush claim forms (open alternative wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternate accepted form uses plain alternatives with 'is ... or ...' (using 'or' and omitting 'consisting of').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix elements of the two forms (e.g., do not combine 'consisting of'/'and' with the 'or' style). The second form should not use 'and.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix the two Markush forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not combine the closed 'selected from the group consisting of ... and' form with the 'is ... or ...' form; mixing forms undermines proper Markush syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explicitly warns: 'Do not mix and match the first form with the second form' — follow one form consistently in the same claim clause to avoid ambiguity or rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members must share a characteristic / belong to a recognized class
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements listed in a Markush group must share a characteristic or property — they should 'belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or an art-recognized class' (MPEP 2173.05(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient if the members are disclosed in the specification to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship; the shared property should be clear from their nature or the prior art. Failure to show a common characteristic can lead to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the shared property in the specification (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practice: explicitly state what shared property or characteristic unites the listed group members in the patent specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the common property in the specification reduces risk of examiner rejection for indefiniteness or lack of proper grouping; if the claimed shared characteristic is too abstract or broad, an examiner may reject and require amendment into multiple dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use closed-group wording to avoid indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'consisting of' with the conjunctive 'and' indicates a closed list, which is important to avoid indefiniteness rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that the closed-group construction 'consisting of ... and' helps avoid an indefiniteness rejection; choose closed wording when you intend a limited, specific set of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other prosecution issues (double-patenting, restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of other issues that may arise with Markush claims — e.g., double-patenting and restriction requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article mentions these as additional concerns to evaluate when using Markush claims and refers practitioners to further guidance (MPEP and other resources) for handling those topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage to illustrate proper drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical example: 'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of lithium, sodium, and potassium' demonstrates both the purpose and form of a Markush claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples like the alkali metal listing to model claim language; examples help show closed-group syntax and when a Markush claim replaces multiple dependent claims.
